title: Tax-Free Versus Tax-Deferred Growth
summary: MATCHED MONEY FIRST → THEN TAX RATE → PICK THE ACCOUNT
subtitle: Six accounts, one question underneath almost all of them: does the tax get paid now, or later?

blocks.text: You’ve now met six registered accounts in this course: the TFSA, RRSP, FHSA, RESP, RDSP and RRIF.
They look like six separate things to memorize. Underneath, almost every one of them answers the same question in one of two ways.
When does the tax get paid: now, or later? Get that straight, and the system stops feeling like a pile of acronyms and starts looking like a set of tools with clear uses.
Put each dollar in the account where it keeps the most for you.
blocks.detail: One simple question about your tax rate now and later sorts out which account fits each goal.
blocks.extra: Section 05 gives you a rough order to follow.

sections.title: The two models, side by side

blocks.text: Tax-free: pay tax now, never again. You put in money that has already been taxed, with no deduction going in. From then on, growth isn’t taxed and withdrawals aren’t taxed. A TFSA works this way. The FHSA works this way too for a qualifying home, and it’s unusual because it also gives you a deduction going in.

Tax-deferred: skip the tax now, pay it later. You get a deduction today, which lowers this year’s tax. The money grows sheltered. But when it comes out, the withdrawal counts as income and is taxed at whatever rate applies then. An RRSP works this way, and so does the RRIF it becomes. The RDSP is also tax-deferred on its growth and government money.
Neither model is better on its own. Which one wins depends on your tax rate now versus your tax rate later.

items.title: TFSA
items.text: No deduction going in. Withdrawals are tax-free.

items.title: RRSP AND RRIF
items.text: Deduction going in. Withdrawals are fully taxed as income.

items.title: FHSA
items.text: Deduction going in. Withdrawals for a qualifying first home are tax-free.

items.title: RESP
items.text: No deduction going in. Your deposits come back tax-free. Growth and grants are taxed to the student, who usually pays little.

items.title: RDSP
items.text: No deduction going in. Growth and government money are taxed to the person the plan is for when they take it out.

items.title: “Tax-free is always better than tax-deferred.”
items.text: Not always. A tax-deferred account gives you a deduction at today’s rate. If today’s rate is high and your retirement rate will be lower, that’s worth a lot. Tax-free wins when your rate today is low and likely to rise. It’s a comparison, not a ranking.

sections.title: The question that answers most of these decisions

blocks.text: CREDIT PULSE SPOTLIGHT: THE QUESTION THAT ANSWERS MOST OF THESE DECISIONS

Ask yourself one thing: is my tax rate higher now, or will it be higher later? If your rate is high now, in your peak earning years on an upper shelf, a deduction is doing real work. Tax-deferred accounts like an RRSP shine here, because you skip tax at a high rate and pay it later at a lower one. If your rate is low now, early in your career, working part-time, on parental leave or partly retired, a deduction isn’t saving you much. Tax-free accounts make more sense, because you pay tax at a cheap rate today and never again. Remember that “later” includes benefits too. RRSP and RRIF withdrawals count as income and can shrink Old Age Security, the Guaranteed Income Supplement and other income-tested benefits. TFSA withdrawals don’t. This one question explains why the same advice can be right for one person and wrong for their neighbour.

sections.title: The account that breaks the pattern

blocks.text: Most accounts pick one model. The FHSA takes both.
You get a deduction going in, like a tax-deferred account. And qualifying withdrawals come out untaxed, like a tax-free one. There’s nothing to pay back either, unlike the Home Buyers’ Plan.
That mix is rare. It’s why, if you qualify for an FHSA, it usually deserves attention before you weigh the other two.
There’s no single answer here, and your own situation matters more than any general rule. But a common order looks like this.

items.title: A small emergency fund first. Keep a few months of costs somewhere easy to reach, such as a high-interest savings account or a TFSA, so a surprise bill doesn’t force you to cash out an RRSP and pay tax.
Employer pension matching first. If your workplace matches what you put in, that’s an instant, guaranteed return before tax even enters the picture.
Government-matched accounts next. RESP grants and RDSP grants and bonds pay more per dollar than almost any tax strategy. If you qualify, they’re hard to beat.
Then the tax-rate question. High shelf now? Lean RRSP. Low shelf now? Lean TFSA. Saving for a first home? The FHSA likely comes first.

blocks.text: Notice that matched accounts come before the tax question. A guaranteed 20% or more from a government grant beats a tax deduction in almost every case.
CREDIT PULSE SPOTLIGHT: THE SECOND QUESTION, WHO INHERITS IT

Now-or-later isn’t the only question behind these accounts. There’s a second, quieter one: what happens to this account the day you die? A TFSA with a spouse named successor holder keeps its tax-free status. With only a beneficiary named, the account closes and the money moves out. A RRIF with a spouse named successor annuitant continues. With only a beneficiary, its full value is generally added to your income in the year you die. An RESP can pass to a sibling. RDSP grants and bonds have their own repayment rules if the plan closes early. Different accounts, same pattern: whether an account passes on intact or turns into a tax bill often comes down to one line on one form, filled in years before anyone needed it.

items.title: “I should pick one account type and put everything there.”
items.text: Most Canadians do better using several, at different life stages and for different goals: a TFSA for flexible savings, an RRSP in peak earning years, an FHSA while a first home is ahead. They’re tools, not teams to pick.

items.title: I know whether my tax rate is likely higher now or later.
I’ve checked for an employer match or a government grant before thinking about tax.
If I’m saving for a first home, I’ve considered the FHSA before anything else.
I understand that RRSP and RRIF withdrawals count as income, and can affect income-tested benefits later.
I’m not treating any one account as best for everyone. The right answer depends on my situation.

sections.title: The same advice, three different people

blocks.text: The same advice, three different people
paragraphs: Three coworkers at a Regina insurance office got the same tip from the same friendly manager, Doug, at the summer barbecue: put everything into your RRSP.
For Ines, forty-eight and at the top of her earning years, it was great advice. Her deduction landed on a high shelf, saving real tax, and her rate in retirement will almost certainly be lower.

For Tomas, twenty-four and in his first year of work, it was weak advice. His income sat on the lowest shelf, so the deduction saved him little. A TFSA would have given him more flexibility and cost him almost nothing in lost tax savings. He had been about to move his whole emergency fund into an RRSP. Instead, he asked Ines what she thought, and she told him to check his shelf first. He kept his emergency fund in a TFSA.

For Grace, thirty-one and saving hard for a first condo, it was the wrong advice entirely. She qualified for an FHSA, which gave her the same deduction plus tax-free withdrawals for the exact goal she was saving for. She opened one the next week.

The twist came at the next barbecue. Doug admitted his own advice had been built for his life: a big salary, a paid-off house and a pension. He hadn’t meant to steer anyone wrong. He just hadn’t asked anyone a single question.
Same sentence, three different people. That year, Doug changed his barbecue tip to a question: “Is your tax rate higher now, or later?”

blocks.text: Almost every registered account answers one question: do you pay tax now, or later? Tax-free accounts cost you tax today and never again. Tax-deferred accounts give you a deduction today and tax you when you withdraw. Which wins depends on whether your tax rate is higher now or later. Government-matched accounts like the RESP and RDSP usually come first, since a guaranteed match beats a deduction.
Ask one question before you follow anyone’s money advice.
blocks.detail: Knowing whether your tax rate is higher now or later lets you choose the right account for every goal.
blocks.extra: Section 08 helps you map your own accounts.

items.title: Write down which shelf you’re on this year, and whether you expect to be higher or lower in retirement.
Check whether any matched money is open to you: an employer pension match, RESP grants, or RDSP grants and bonds. Those come first.
List the accounts you have open, and mark each one tax-free or tax-deferred. If they’re all one kind, ask whether that still fits your life.

blocks.text: Worksheet: your account map

items.title: Tax-free growth
items.text: You put in money that has already been taxed. Growth and withdrawals are never taxed.

items.title: Tax-deferred growth
items.text: Deposits are deducted now. Growth is sheltered, and withdrawals are taxed as income later.

items.title: Marginal rate
items.text: The rate on your next dollar of income. The number that decides how much a deduction is worth.

items.title: Matched contribution
items.text: Money an employer or the government adds on top of yours. Usually worth putting first.

questions: Which accounts do you have open, and is each one tax-free or tax-deferred?
Is your tax rate likely higher now, or later?
Is there matched money you qualify for but aren’t claiming?
Do you have an emergency fund you can reach without cashing out an RRSP?
If you’re saving for a first home, do you have an FHSA?
Which account will your next dollar go into, and why?
